Chapter 2: The Pull of Negative News and the Reality of Progress
Have you ever noticed how bad news just grabs your attention, almost like it’s impossible to look away?
That’s not by accident. It’s something experts call the “negativity instinct.” Our minds are naturally drawn to threats and dangers—a survival trait that helped our ancestors, but today, it can make the world seem far scarier and more chaotic than it actually is.
Think about it: when you scroll through headlines or overhear people talking, what kinds of stories really stand out? Usually, it’s the ones about violence, disease, or disaster. Positive changes—like falling child mortality, more kids learning to read, or greater access to clean water—hardly ever get top billing.
And what does that do? It creates this constant sense that everything’s getting worse, even though, in reality, most measures of human well-being are quietly improving all the time.
Here’s why it happens. Our brains lock onto negative events. They’re more memorable. They spark stronger emotions, triggering worry and concern. After a while, it’s easy to lose sight of the bigger picture, and all the progress happening behind the scenes just gets drowned out.
But if you zoom out and look at the long-term trends, a totally different story comes into focus. Over the last hundred years, people are living longer, extreme poverty is way down, and more children than ever are in school.
These changes didn’t happen overnight. They’re the result of slow, steady work—generation after generation pushing things forward.
So how do you resist that pull toward negativity?
First, try looking for long-term trends, not just what’s in the news right now.
Second, compare today’s numbers to the past, instead of focusing only on the setbacks.
And third, remind yourself that real progress is usually gradual and steady, while problems can seem sudden and overwhelming.
Take global health, for instance. One outbreak makes headlines, but the real story is that, thanks to vaccines, better nutrition, and cleaner water, millions of lives have been saved—though you rarely hear about it.
If you make a conscious effort to spot the signs of progress, you’ll start to see a more balanced, hopeful world. That doesn’t mean ignoring real problems. It just means putting them in perspective—recognizing how far we’ve come, while still working to make things better.
